children: New Delhi, Sept. 21 -- India's leading automakers and auto component manufacturers are increasingly relying on temporary workers, with non-permanent workers making up nearly 90% of the total worker count at several companies.

A Mint review of the annual reports of leading auto companies shows that the share of temporary workers has risen sharply over the past four fiscal years, as companies expanded production, added shifts and increased factory capacity to capitalise on growth in the Indian market.

The trend is visible across several major automakers, with temporary workers accounting for 83-92% of the workforce at Maruti Suzuki, Mahindra & Mahindra Ltd, Tata Motors, Hyundai Motor India and Hero MotoCorp, as well as homegrown auto component makers Samvardhana Motherson and Sona Comstar.

The shift towards a predominantly temporary workforce gives companies greater flexibility in managing costs and adjusting staffing levels to production cycles. However, it also exposes them to risks related to labour availability, workforce continuity and potential disruptions arising from wage disputes and protests.

"Contractual manpower has given automakers flexibility to manage costs and adjust manpower with production cycles. But when 85-90% of the shopfloor is non-permanent, maintaining continuity of skills, experience, productivity and shopfloor discipline becomes much harder," said Vinay Piparsania, founder of MillenStrat Advisory and Research.
The workers include those involved in production on manufacturing lines as well as employees in non-production roles within factory premises, including logistics, maintenance, sales and dispatch.

The growing reliance on temporary workers comes as labour shortages and wage-related protests have disrupted industrial activity in parts of Haryana and Uttar Pradesh this year. Workers' demands have included higher wages and permanent employment contracts, bringing greater attention to the increasing share of non-permanent workers in auto manufacturing.

Maruti Suzuki, India's largest carmaker, saw the share of temporary workers rise from 71% at the end of fiscal year 2023 (FY23) to 87% in fiscal year 2026, as it expanded its factory operations. The company added nearly 30,000 non-permanent workers during the period. The increase also reflects the amalgamation of Suzuki Motor Gujarat (SMG) with Maruti Suzuki in FY26. SMG operated the company's largest manufacturing facility, in Hansalpur, Gujarat.

At Mahindra & Mahindra, the share of temporary workers increased from 77% in FY23 to 86% in FY26, with the company adding nearly 30,000 workers and almost doubling its temporary workforce. Tata Motors' passenger vehicle business reported a temporary workforce share of 85% in FY26, while the figure for Hyundai Motor India was 83%. Comparable FY23 figures for the two companies were not available.
At Hero MotoCorp, India's largest two-wheeler maker, the share of temporary workers rose from 82% to 87% during the same period, with the company adding nearly 10,000 workers.
Not all automakers have a sizable temporary workforce. At Bajaj Auto, non-permanent workers accounted for 4% of the total workforce, while TVS Motor reported no temporary workers at its factories.

A sharper shift was visible at Samvardhana Motherson, the country's largest auto component maker, where the share of temporary workers increased from 35% in FY23 to 88% in FY26. The company was among those whose production was disrupted by protests at facilities in Noida.

Although companies do not clearly disclose differences in wages between permanent and temporary workers, their disclosures suggest that shorter worker tenures provide greater flexibility in managing labour costs.
Piparsania said the shift towards a predominantly non-permanent workforce should be viewed as an operational issue.

"The labour shortages and worker protests this year are two sides of the same issue-the need to balance workforce flexibility with stability. When a large part of the workforce is transient, both continuity and availability can become challenges, with a direct impact on production," he said.
In July, Mahindra & Mahindra management said some of its suppliers had been affected by labour shortages, curtailing production of some models.

"We were impacted. At least three or four of our suppliers were impacted pretty badly by labour shortages, first because of the gas shortage issue, then elections, and then migration of labour to the north where wage rates had gone up," said Rajesh Jejurikar, executive director and chief executive (auto and farm sector) at Mahindra & Mahindra.

Auto manufacturing hubs had already witnessed protests over higher inflation amid the West Asia war and demands for higher minimum wages. The protests prompted the Haryana and Uttar Pradesh governments to raise minimum wage levels.
According to Ashim Sharma, senior partner at Nomura Research Institute, that automobile companies could have invested in automating lines as seen globally for enhancing output per employee,

"Although leading amongst industries in India, automation at Indian automotive factories remains low when compared to other global markets which has driven the rising share of the contractual workforce. Companies could gain a higher competitive advantage in global value chains through investment in automation and robotics, " he said. title: Temporary workers account for nearly 90% of workforce at several auto companies
